label: thm:fractional_matching
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:fractional_matching}
Let $1\leq d\leq k$ be integers and let $\mathcal{H}$ be the hypergraph with $\delta_d (\mathcal{H})> \Big(1-\big(1-\frac{1}{k}\big)^{k-d}\Big)\frac{n^{k-d}}{(k-d)!}$. Then $\mathcal{H}$ has a perfect fractional matching.

label: lemma:safe_move
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lemma:safe_move}
Unless $S$ is deterministic, there is some $i$ such that replacing $X_i$ by $u_i$ is a safe move.
head: environment

title: Proof
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
In this proof, we will show that replacing $X_i$ by $u_i$ is a safe move precisely when $X_i$ is positively correlated with the variable $S$ conditioned on $S<\lambda$. This makes sense: removing such a variable $X_i$ certainly decreases the expectation $\mathbb{E}[S|S<\lambda]$, and consequently increases the difference $r(S)=\lambda-\mathbb{E}[S|S<\lambda]$. We now give the details.

The key observation is that for every random variable $X_i$ appearing in $S$ we have $\operatorname{Cov}(S, X_i|S<\lambda)=(v_i-u_i)\mathbb P[X_i=u_i|S<\lambda](r(S_i)-r(S))$, where $u_i<v_i$ is the support of $X_i$.

Once we prove this, we simply write \vspace{-0.1cm}\[0\leq \operatorname{Var}(S|S<\lambda)=\sum_{i=1}^n \operatorname{Cov}(S, X_i|S<\lambda)=\sum_{i=1}^n (v_i-u_i)\mathbb P[X_i=u_i|S<\lambda](r(S_i)-r(S)),\] where the sums run over the remaining random summands. Since the coefficients $(v_i-u_i)\mathbb P[X_i=u_i|S<\lambda]$ are positive, this shows that for some $i$ we have $r(S_i)\geq r(S)$, ultimately showing there is a safe move.

Let us now prove the key observation. We can write $X_i=u_i+(v_i-u_i)B$ for a Bernoulli variable $B$, and so $\operatorname{Cov}(S, X_i|S<\lambda)=(v_i-u_i)\operatorname{Cov}(S, B|S<\lambda)$. The latter covariance can be computed as follows
\vspace{-0.1cm}
\begin{align*}
\operatorname{Cov}\!\big(S, B\big|S<\lambda\big)\!=\!-\!\operatorname{Cov}\!\big(S, 1\!-\!B\big| S\!<\!\lambda\big)\!&=\!\mathbb{E}\big[S\big|S\!<\!\lambda\big]\mathbb{E}\big[1\!-\!B\big|S\!<\!\lambda\big]\!-\!\mathbb{E}\big[S(1-B)\big|S<\lambda\big]\\
&=\!\mathbb{E}\big[S\big|S\!<\!\lambda\big]\mathbb P\big[B\!=\!0\big|S\!<\!\lambda\big]\!-\!\mathbb{E}\big[S\big|B\!=\!0\text{ and }S\!<\!\lambda\big]\mathbb P\big[B\!=\!0\big|S\!<\!\lambda\big]
\end{align*}
When $B=0$ we have $X_i=u_i$ and $S=S_i$. This means that 
$\mathbb{E}\big[S\big|B\!=\!0\text{ and }S\!<\!\lambda\big]=\mathbb{E}[S_i|S_i<\lambda]$ and therefore
$\mathbb{E}\big[S\big|S\!<\!\lambda\big]\!-\!\mathbb{E}\big[S\big|B\!=\!0\text{ and }S\!<\!\lambda\big]=r(S_i)-r(S)$.
Putting all of the above steps together, we get \[\operatorname{Cov}(S, X_i|S<\lambda)=(v_i-u_i)\operatorname{Cov}(S, B|S<\lambda)= (v_i-u_i)\mathbb P[X_i=u_i|S<\lambda](r(S_i)-r(S)).\qedhere\]

label: lemma:two_values
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lemma:two_values}
Let $X_i$ be a random variable whose support includes at least three different values. Then, $X_i$ can be replaced by another random variable whose support includes at most two of the values from the support of $X_i$ and has the same mean. Moreover, $\mathbb P[\sum_{j=1}^n X_j<n+\delta]$ does not increase through this replacement.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $T=\sum_{j\ne i}X_j$. By standard approximation arguments, we may assume $X_i$ has finite support, say $v_1, \dots, v_m$. Let us denote $p_k=\mathbb P[X_i=v_k]$ and $q_k=\mathbb P[T+v_k<n+\delta]$. By the law of total probability, we have 
\[\mathbb P\Big[\sum_{j=1}^n X_j<n+\delta\Big]=\sum_{k=1}^m \mathbb P[X_i=v_k]\mathbb P\big[T+v_k<n+\delta\big]=\sum_{k=1}^m p_kq_k.\]
Hence, our goal is to minimize the linear program $\sum_{k=1}^m p_kq_k$ over the variables $p_1, \dots, p_m$, while preserving $\mathbb{E} X_i=1$. This means that our program is subject to constraints $\sum_{k=1}^m p_k=1$ and $\sum_{k=1}^m p_kv_k=1$. The program is feasible (since we already know $X_i$ satisfies the constraints), and since it has two constraints, its optimal solution can have at most two nonzero values among $p_1, \dots, p_m$, meaning that the support of $X_i$ can be reduced to only two values without increasing $\mathbb P[\sum_{j=1}^n X_j<n+\delta]$.\hspace{5cm}$\square$
